1.title: Cybersecurity Concepts: CIA, AAA, Non-Repudiation and Privacy
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Cybersecurity Concepts: C I A, A A A, Non-Repudiation and Privacy. It covers the exam area one. Security Principles. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. one point one Understand cybersecurity concepts: Confidentiality. Integrity. Availability. Authentication, Authorization, Accounting (A A A). Non-repudiation. Privacy. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: one. Security Principles (twenty-four percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: The CIA triad
1.text: The C I A triad. The figure shows this: The C I A triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability, with an example control for each.

1.title: The CIA triad, continued
1.text: The C I A triad. Confidentiality. Meaning: Only authorized people can read the data. Example controls: Encryption, access control, data classification. Attack that breaks it: Disclosure: a data breach, eavesdropping. Integrity. Meaning: Data is accurate and unaltered. Example controls: Hashing, digital signatures, version control, input checks. Attack that breaks it: Alteration: tampering, model poisoning.

1.title: The CIA triad, continued
1.text: The C I A triad. Availability. Meaning: Systems and data are there when needed. Example controls: Redundancy, backups, patching, D dos (distributed denial of service) protection. Attack that breaks it: Destruction or denial: ransomware, D dos. The opposite of C I A is D A D: Disclosure, Alteration, Destruction (or denial). Exam tip: Match the goal to the symptom. Leak equals confidentiality. Changed or fake data equals integrity. Outage equals availability. A hash proves integrity, not secrecy.

1.title: AI and the triad
1.text: A I and the triad. Foundational A I concepts are part of the outline in every domain. Confidentiality. Protect the privacy of training data; staff must not paste secrets into public A I tools. Integrity. Prevent model poisoning by controlling the training data. Availability. A model or its service that is down or degraded hurts operations.

1.title: AAA: authentication, authorization, accounting
1.text: A A A: authentication, authorization, accounting. Authentication. Question: Who are you? Examples: Password, token, fingerprint, multi-factor authentication. Authorization. Question: What may you do? Examples: Permissions, roles, access control lists. Accounting. Question: What did you do? Examples: Logs, audit trails, session records. Authentication factors: something you know (password, P I N), something you have (token, smart card, phone), something you are (fingerprint, face). M F A uses factors from two or more different categories; two passwords are not M F A. Exam tip: Authentication comes first, then authorization, then accounting. Logs support accountability because they tie actions to an identity.

1.title: Non-repudiation
1.text: Non-repudiation. Non-repudiation means a person cannot credibly deny an action such as sending a message or approving a payment. Digital signature. Proves who signed and that the data was not changed (made with the sender's private key). Audit logs. Tie the action to an identity and a time. Strong authentication. Makes it hard to claim that someone else acted. A A A and non-repudiation also keep actions of A I tools traceable.

1.title: Privacy
1.text: Privacy. Privacy is the right of individuals to control how their personal information is collected, used and shared. Security protects the data; privacy decides what may be done with it. Personally identifiable information (P I I). Data that identifies a person, alone or combined (name, I D number, email). Data minimization. Collect and keep only what is needed. Consent and purpose. Use data only for the stated purpose. Privacy laws. For example G D P R; they set duties and fines (Module three). Exam tip: Security without privacy is possible; privacy without security is not. A system can be secure and still misuse personal data.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A laptop with customer records is stolen and the disk is not encrypted. Which security goal is most directly harmed? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Confidentiality, because unauthorized people can read the data. Unauthorized disclosure of data harms confidentiality; encryption would have protected it.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An attacker changes the amount of a bank transfer while it travels over the network. Which goal does this attack violate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Integrity, because the data was altered in transit. Unauthorized alteration violates integrity.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A hospital system is encrypted by ransomware and doctors cannot open patient files. Which goal is harmed first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Availability, because the data cannot be accessed. Ransomware denies access to the data, which is an availability failure.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A user logs in with a password and then approves a prompt on a phone. What does this illustrate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Multi-factor authentication with two different factors. A password (know) plus a phone (have) are two categories of factor.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A manager signs a contract with a digital signature and later says she never signed it. Which concept makes the denial hard to defend? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Non-repudiation provided by the signature. A digital signature supports non-repudiation: the signer cannot credibly deny it.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A company encrypts customer data but uses it for marketing without the customers' knowledge. Which concept is violated? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Privacy, because the data is used beyond its stated purpose. Privacy is about how personal data is used and shared, even when it is well protected.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does the C in C I A stand for? Answer: Confidentiality. Question two. Which control mainly supports integrity? Answer: Hashing (and digital signatures). Question three. What question does authorization answer? Answer: What may you do?

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name the three authentication factor categories. Answer: Something you know, have and are. Question five. What does D A D stand for? Answer: Disclosure, alteration, destruction (or denial). Question six. What does non-repudiation prevent? Answer: A person denying an action they took.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. C I A: confidentiality (secrecy), integrity (accuracy), availability (access). D A D: disclosure, alteration, destruction or denial. A A A: authentication (who), authorization (what), accounting (what you did). M F A: two or more different factor categories. Non-repudiation: digital signatures and logs; no credible denial. Privacy: control over personal data; P I I; data minimization.
